prompt.context_jp: 「小野寺くん___ プレゼントくれたのね」
prompt.prompt_jp: 小野寺くん___ プレゼントくれたのね
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi is recalling who gave him the present. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: The point of this line is identifying the giver — it was Onodera who gave the present. That identificational focus takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make Onodera the already-known topic and shift focus elsewhere, which doesn't fit when the giver's identity itself is the news. に would mean 'to Onodera,' flipping the direction.

contrast_examples.jp: 小野寺くんがくれた。
contrast_examples.en: Onodera is the one who gave it. (identifying the giver)

contrast_examples.jp: 小野寺くんはくれた。
contrast_examples.en: As for Onodera, he gave it (contrasted with others).

prompt.context_jp: 「なんか 意外と ああいうタイプ___急に爆発して 凶悪犯罪とか起こしたりするじゃん」
prompt.prompt_jp: ああいうタイプ___急に爆発して 凶悪犯罪とか起こしたりするじゃん
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi is making a general claim about 'that type of person' as the subject of a sudden action. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: Inside the relative-clause-like description 'the type that suddenly snaps and commits crimes,' が picks out the subject that performs the action. The focus is on identifying which kind of person does this.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to topicalize 'that type,' but the clause is embedded as a characterizing description — a neutral-description が is natural here. で would mark means/location, not a subject.

contrast_examples.jp: ああいうタイプが爆発する。
contrast_examples.en: It's that type who snaps. (identifying)

contrast_examples.jp: ああいうタイプは静かだ。
contrast_examples.en: As for that type, they are quiet. (topic + general property)

prompt.context_jp: 「ていうのも その人 毎回 帰るの___ すっごい早いんですよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: その人 毎回 帰るの___ すっごい早いんですよ
prompt.prompt_en: Yumi is introducing a surprising observation about Onodera's leaving. Which particle fits the nominalized subject?

feedback.correct_en: '帰るの' (the act of leaving) is being newly presented as remarkably fast — a neutral description introducing a surprising fact, which takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would imply 'as for leaving (compared to other things), it's fast,' which doesn't match this excited revelation. を can't mark a nominalized subject of an adjective.

contrast_examples.jp: 帰るのが早い。
contrast_examples.en: His leaving is fast. (observation / new info)

contrast_examples.jp: 帰るのは早いけど、来るのは遅い。
contrast_examples.en: Leaving-wise he's fast, but coming-wise he's slow. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 「それで 私たちの間で 宇宙人説___出てたんですね」
prompt.prompt_jp: 私たちの間で 宇宙人説___出てたんですね
prompt.prompt_en: Yumi is reporting that an 'alien theory' arose. Which particle marks this newly-introduced theory?

feedback.correct_en: The theory is being introduced into the conversation for the first time — an existence/emergence reading that takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose the alien theory as already known, undercutting the reveal. に marks location/goal and doesn't fit.

contrast_examples.jp: 宇宙人説が出てた。
contrast_examples.en: An alien theory came up. (new emergence)

contrast_examples.jp: 宇宙人説はもう却下された。
contrast_examples.en: As for the alien theory, it's already been rejected. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 「ものすごいスピードで 移動する男性を見たっていう人___ 何人かいたんですね」
prompt.prompt_jp: …男性を見たっていう人___ 何人かいたんですね
prompt.prompt_en: Kishimoto is reporting the existence of several witnesses. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: This is a classic existence sentence ('there were several people who...') — the subject of いる in a presentational statement takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn 'such people' into a known topic, odd when their existence is the news. も ('also') needs a prior comparable group, which isn't set up.

contrast_examples.jp: 見たっていう人が何人かいた。
contrast_examples.en: There were several people who said they saw him.

contrast_examples.jp: 見たっていう人は少ない。
contrast_examples.en: As for people who said they saw him, they're few. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 「あ～ 小野寺くん___… あした 朝番だから 7時には いると思いますけど」
prompt.prompt_jp: 小野寺くん___ あした 朝番だから 7時にはいると思いますけど
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi is answering a question about Onodera specifically. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: Onodera has already been named by the interviewer; Kiyomi is now commenting about him as the established topic. That's prototypical topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would re-introduce Onodera as new information, odd when he's exactly what was just asked about. を can't mark the subject of a copula/stative predicate.

contrast_examples.jp: 小野寺くんは明日 朝番です。
contrast_examples.en: As for Onodera, he's on the morning shift tomorrow. (answering about him)

contrast_examples.jp: 明日 朝番なのは小野寺くんが です。
contrast_examples.en: The one on morning shift tomorrow is Onodera. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 「いや 前に 小野寺くん___ 枕を買い替えたいって話してたのよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 前に 小野寺くん___ 枕を買い替えたいって話してたのよ
prompt.prompt_en: The manager is recalling who had mentioned wanting a new pillow. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: He's recalling a specific past event and introducing the fact that Onodera (not someone else) was the one who said this — new-information が inside a subordinate 'って' clause.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark Onodera as an ongoing topic, but here the manager is dredging up a one-time episode and specifying the speaker. に would make Onodera the addressee, flipping the meaning.

contrast_examples.jp: 小野寺くんが話してた。
contrast_examples.en: Onodera was the one who told me. (identifying the speaker)

contrast_examples.jp: 小野寺くんは枕の話ばかりする。
contrast_examples.en: Onodera always talks about pillows. (habitual topic)

prompt.context_jp: 「フロント___支配人と清美だけが残された」
prompt.prompt_jp: フロント___は支配人と清美だけが残された
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator contrasts the front desk (where two remain) with elsewhere (where Yumi went). Which particle attaches to フロント?

feedback.correct_en: Existence/remaining takes に for the location ('フロントには…残された'). The は piggy-backs on に to add a contrastive-topic nuance (at the front desk, as opposed to elsewhere).
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks the site of an action, not of existence/remaining. を would mark a path or object, which doesn't fit 残される.

contrast_examples.jp: フロントには二人が残った。
contrast_examples.en: At the front desk, two people remained.

contrast_examples.jp: フロントで話し合った。
contrast_examples.en: They talked at the front desk. (location of action)

prompt.context_jp: 「掌の上のそれ___、まぎれもなく本物の十円玉だった」
prompt.prompt_jp: 掌の上のそれ___ まぎれもなく本物の十円玉だった
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator describes the coin on the manager's palm, already referenced. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: 'That thing on his palm' is already in the discourse — referring back to the just-handed-over coin. Characterizing it ('…was unmistakably real') takes topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would re-introduce the coin as new information, but it's already the focal object. を is impossible with the copula.

contrast_examples.jp: それは本物だった。
contrast_examples.en: That (established referent) was real. (topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 本物が一枚あった。
contrast_examples.en: There was one real one. (new existential subject)

prompt.context_jp: 「清美の背中に、いやな予感___針で刺されたようにひどく痛い緊張として走った」
prompt.prompt_jp: いやな予感___針で刺されたようにひどく痛い緊張として走った
prompt.prompt_en: A bad premonition suddenly runs through Kiyomi. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: A sensation suddenly arising ('a bad feeling shot through her') is a prototypical neutral-description event, taking が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat 'bad premonition' as a known topic, dulling the sudden sensory jolt. を doesn't fit the intransitive 走る.

contrast_examples.jp: 寒気がした。
contrast_examples.en: A chill ran through me. (sudden sensation)

contrast_examples.jp: 予感はよく当たる。
contrast_examples.en: As for premonitions, they often come true. (topic/general)

prompt.context_jp: 「廊下を歩く足取り___、緊張のあまり、微かにびっこを引くように重かった」
prompt.prompt_jp: 廊下を歩く足取り___ 緊張のあまり 微かにびっこを引くように重かった
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator characterizes Takahashi's gait as heavy. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is characterizing a specific referenced thing (his gait at this moment) with a stative descriptor ('was heavy'). Topic は fits that comment structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present his footsteps as fresh information, but the sentence is a reflective description, not an event report. で marks means/location.

contrast_examples.jp: 足取りは重かった。
contrast_examples.en: His gait was heavy. (characterizing)

contrast_examples.jp: 足取りが乱れた。
contrast_examples.en: His footsteps grew unsteady. (event — new info)

prompt.context_jp: 「…で 思い返してみたら "実は サイン___てた" みたいな感じでさ」
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi is quoting the stock phrase coworkers use in interviews about criminals: 'he was actually ___ signals.'

feedback.correct_en: 'サインを出す' is the fixed collocation for 'giving/dropping signs or hints.' It's the standard idiom in the exact TV cliché Takahashi is parodying.
feedback.incorrect_en: 作る (make) and 書く (write) treat サイン as a physical autograph. 見せる is possible but less idiomatic for 'warning signs' in this cliché.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼はサインを出していた。
contrast_examples.en: He had been giving off signs.

contrast_examples.jp: 色紙にサインを書いた。
contrast_examples.en: He wrote an autograph on the shikishi. (literal signature)

prompt.context_jp: 「こんだけクリームまみれなのに 全く___がしないんですよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: こんだけクリームまみれなのに 全く___がしないんですよ
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi is praising a parfait — despite all the cream, you don't get this sensation.

feedback.correct_en: '胸焼けがする' is the set expression for heartburn, exactly the complaint rich creamy food usually causes.
feedback.incorrect_en: 気分がする isn't a standalone phrase. 食欲がしない isn't idiomatic (you'd say 食欲がない). お腹がする is ungrammatical.

contrast_examples.jp: 胸焼けがする。
contrast_examples.en: I have heartburn.

contrast_examples.jp: 食欲がない。
contrast_examples.en: I have no appetite. (different pattern — ない, not しない)

prompt.context_jp: 「このままだと 何の罪もない小野寺くんが ホテル内で ___扱いになっちゃいますよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: ホテル内で ___扱いになっちゃいますよ
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi warns that innocent Onodera will end up treated like what?

feedback.correct_en: '腫れ物扱い' ('treating like a swelling/sore') is the idiomatic phrase for walking on eggshells around someone — the exact word Kiyomi uses.
feedback.incorrect_en: お荷物扱い means 'treating as a burden' (different nuance — being useless, not feared). お客様扱い is the opposite (overly polite). 厄介者 is close but less idiomatic with 扱い here.

contrast_examples.jp: 腫れ物に触るように扱う。
contrast_examples.en: Treat someone like they'll break — walking on eggshells.

contrast_examples.jp: お荷物扱いされる。
contrast_examples.en: Be treated like a burden/deadweight.

prompt.context_jp: 「街録の証言と うまく合わせて 都市伝説っぽい___にすれば いけるんじゃない？」
prompt.prompt_jp: 都市伝説っぽい___にすれば いけるんじゃない？
prompt.prompt_en: Kishimoto suggests framing it with an urban-legend-flavored ___ (angle).

feedback.correct_en: '切り口' is the standard media/journalism term for 'angle' or 'approach' when framing a story.
feedback.incorrect_en: 入り口 (entrance) and 出口 (exit) are literal passage words. 糸口 means 'clue/lead' (for solving something), not 'angle for framing content.'

contrast_examples.jp: 新しい切り口で特集を作る。
contrast_examples.en: Make a feature with a new angle.

contrast_examples.jp: 事件の糸口をつかむ。
contrast_examples.en: Grab a lead on the case.

prompt.context_jp: 「はい しかも 結構 ___てて」
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi warns Takahashi that the TV crew is really ___ (hooked on) the story.

feedback.correct_en: '食いつく' ('to bite onto / latch onto') is the standard idiom for a journalist or audience eagerly latching onto a story — exactly matching the original line.
feedback.incorrect_en: 飛びつく suggests leaping at something (more physical reaction). 乗っかる means to go along with, not to be hooked. はまる is 'to be addicted,' needing more time; it doesn't fit this immediate reaction.

contrast_examples.jp: 記者が食いついてきた。
contrast_examples.en: The reporters took the bait.

contrast_examples.jp: 話に飛びついた。
contrast_examples.en: He jumped at the story. (impulsive)

prompt.context_jp: Kishimoto is politely asking the hotel manager if interviewing staff would be okay.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds most natural for a TV producer softly asking permission on-site?

choices.text: もし ご迷惑でなければ 従業員の方にも インタビューさせていただけないかなぁと思いまして
迷惑じゃなかったら 従業員にも インタビューさせてくれませんか
従業員にインタビューしたいです。いいですか

feedback.correct_en: Option A uses the hedged, humble pattern 'させていただけないかなぁと思いまして' plus 'ご迷惑でなければ' — the register expected when a producer approaches a business owner on the spot.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B is plain-polite but drops the honorific prefixes and hedging that make the request feel non-pushy. Option C is too direct and sounds abrupt for a cold request to a stranger.

contrast_examples.jp: ご迷惑でなければ、お話を伺えればと思いまして。
contrast_examples.en: If it wouldn't be a bother, I was hoping to hear from you.

contrast_examples.jp: インタビューしたいんですけど。
contrast_examples.en: I'd like to interview you. (casual request)

prompt.context_jp: Kiyomi worries that even if Onodera denies the accusation, he'll be railroaded into it anyway.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural for 'I feel like he'll be pushed in that direction'?

choices.text: 強引に そっちのほうに持っていかれそうな 気もするんですよね
強引に そっちのほうに運ばれそうな 気もするんですよね
強引に そっちのほうに行かされそうな 気もするんですよね

feedback.correct_en: '話を持っていく' / '〜に持っていかれる' is the idiomatic way to say 'steer a narrative toward X.' The passive '持っていかれる' captures 'being swept into that framing.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 運ばれる is literal transport, not conversational steering. 行かされる is causative-passive 'be made to go,' which sounds like physical movement, not narrative pressure.

contrast_examples.jp: 話をそっちに持っていかれた。
contrast_examples.en: They steered the conversation that way.

contrast_examples.jp: 荷物を運ばれた。
contrast_examples.en: The luggage was carried. (physical)

prompt.context_jp: Kishimoto opens his interview question about recent personal news.
prompt.prompt_en: Which word order sounds most natural for a TV interviewer opening a question?

choices.text: 最近 身の回りで起こった 個人的なニュースとかって ありますか？
個人的なニュースとかって 最近 身の回りで起こった ありますか？
ありますか 身の回りで起こった 最近 個人的なニュースとかって？

feedback.correct_en: The adverbial '最近' naturally leads, followed by the modifier clause '身の回りで起こった' modifying '個人的なニュース,' then the question '〜ありますか' at the end — standard Japanese ordering.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B breaks up the noun phrase so '身の回りで起こった' can't properly modify 'ニュース.' Option C fronts the verb, which is impossible for a Japanese declarative/interrogative predicate.

contrast_examples.jp: 最近あった出来事ってありますか。
contrast_examples.en: Have you had any recent events?

contrast_examples.jp: ありますか最近あった出来事。
contrast_examples.en: (Ungrammatical word order in standard Japanese.)

prompt.context_jp: Takahashi, after revealing he's an alien, asks his boss to keep treating him as before.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing fits a nervous subordinate making a careful request to his manager?

choices.text: 今までどおり 接していただけると助かります
今までどおり 接してくれると助かる
今までどおり 接してください、お願いします

feedback.correct_en: '〜ていただけると助かります' is the standard polite, deferential pattern for asking a superior a favor — exactly matching Takahashi's careful register with the manager.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B drops into casual plain form, inappropriate upward. Option C sounds like a direct command softened with お願いします — less tactful and more imposing than the hedged conditional.

contrast_examples.jp: ご協力いただけると助かります。
contrast_examples.en: It would help if you could cooperate. (polite request)

contrast_examples.jp: 協力してくれると助かる。
contrast_examples.en: It'd help if you cooperate. (casual, downward)
